status: DRAFT: not yet reviewed, pretested or calibrated. Facts marked verify=true need checking against a primary source before use.

conventions.codes: Options are listed in code order 0..K-1. Code K-1 is the pole named in high_pole. Display order is randomized per person between forward and reverse; codes never change.
always_appended: None of these fit my view (optional: tell us why)
I don't know enough about this to say
firmness_followup: It really depends on the details

items.stem: Which comes closest to what you think the law on abortion should be?
items.scope: Pick the rule you'd want in most situations. You'll be able to add exceptions next.
options: Legal for any reason at any point in pregnancy
Legal for any reason until about the point of viability (around 24 weeks); after that, only for serious risks to the woman's health
Legal for any reason in about the first 12 to 15 weeks; after that, only in specific circumstances
Legal only in specific circumstances, such as rape, incest, or a threat to the woman's life or health
Legal only to save the woman's life
Never legal

definitions.text: The point in pregnancy after which a fetus could survive outside the womb with medical care, usually placed at around 22 to 24 weeks.
definitions.source: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, periviability guidance

items.stem: Under the rule you picked, should abortion also be legal in each of these cases, at any point in pregnancy?
options: Yes
No

cases.text: The pregnancy threatens the woman's life
The pregnancy seriously threatens the woman's health, but not her life
The pregnancy resulted from rape or incest
The fetus has a condition that means it will die before or shortly after birth

items.stem: What should the federal minimum wage be?
items.scope: This is the national floor. States could still set higher minimums.
items.context: The federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour and has not changed since 2009.
options: $20 an hour or more, rising with inflation each year
About $15 an hour, rising with inflation each year
About $10 to $12 an hour
Keep it at $7.25 an hour
No federal minimum; leave it to states and employers

facts.claim: Federal minimum wage is $7.25/hour, unchanged since July 24, 2009
facts.source: US Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division

items.stem: Which comes closest to how you think Americans should get health insurance?
items.scope: Think about the system as a whole, not your own plan.
options: One government plan covers everyone; private insurance plays little or no role
Everyone can choose a government plan or private insurance (a public option)
Mostly private insurance, with government programs for older people, people with low incomes, and those who can't get covered otherwise (roughly today's system)
Mostly private insurance, with smaller government programs than today
Private insurance or paying directly; the government does not provide coverage

definitions.text: A health plan run by the government that anyone can choose to buy instead of a private plan.

items.stem: How should federal income taxes change for people earning more than $1 million a year?
items.scope: Assume the money raised or lost changes the federal budget, not your own taxes.
options: Raise them a lot
Raise them somewhat
Keep them about the same
Lower them somewhat
Lower them a lot

items.stem: Which comes closest to what the federal government should do about climate change?
items.scope: Each option includes its likely cost. Pick the one whose tradeoff you'd accept.
options: Require fast, deep cuts in greenhouse gas emissions, even if energy prices rise noticeably
Require gradual cuts in emissions, accepting small increases in energy prices
Fund research and offer tax credits for clean energy, but not require cuts
Take no specific action on climate change

items.stem: Which comes closest to the rules you want for an adult buying a handgun?
items.scope: Think about a typical adult with no criminal record or history of serious mental illness.
items.context: Under current federal law, licensed gun dealers must run a background check; most private sales between individuals do not require one.
options: Ban handgun sales to most civilians
Require a license that includes safety training, plus a background check for every sale
Require a background check for every sale, including private sales, but no license
Keep current federal law
Fewer federal rules than today, such as ending required background checks

facts.claim: Federal background checks are required for sales by federally licensed dealers, not most private sales
facts.source: Gun Control Act of 1968; Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act (1993); ATF

definitions.text: A check of federal records to confirm the buyer is not legally barred from owning a gun, for example because of a felony conviction.
definitions.source: FBI National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS)

items.stem: Millions of people live in the US without legal immigration status. What should happen to most of them?
items.scope: Think about the typical person in this group: someone who has lived here for several years and has no serious criminal record. You'll be asked about other groups next.
options: Let them stay and apply for citizenship without major penalties
Let them stay and apply for citizenship after requirements such as paying a fine and passing a background check
Let them stay and work legally, but not become citizens
Let them work here for a limited time, then require them to leave
Require them to leave, starting with people with criminal records
Remove all of them as quickly as possible

facts.claim: Pew estimates 14 million unauthorized immigrants as of July 2023 (a record), with a likely decline of up to 1 million in the first half of 2025; DHS estimated about 11 million for January 2022
facts.source: Pew Research Center, 'U.S. Unauthorized Immigrant Population Reached a Record 14 Million in 2023' (Aug 21, 2025); DHS Office of Homeland Security Statistics
facts.note: Pew figures verified 2026-10-12; DHS figure not re-checked. Stem deliberately says 'millions' so the item doesn't date quickly.

definitions.text: People who entered the US without authorization, or who entered legally but stayed after their permission expired.

items.stem: Compared with your last answer, should these groups be treated more leniently, the same, or more strictly?
options: More leniently
The same
More strictly

cases.text: People brought to the US as young children
People who arrived in the last two years
People convicted of a serious crime in the US

items.stem: When colleges choose among qualified applicants, should an applicant's race be considered?
items.scope: Answer about what you think should happen, regardless of what current law allows.
items.context: In 2023 the Supreme Court ruled that colleges may not use race as a factor in admissions.
options: Yes, as one important factor, to increase diversity
Yes, but only as a minor factor, such as a tie-breaker
No, but colleges can consider economic hardship instead
No, colleges should not consider race or other group characteristics at all

facts.claim: Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023) ended race-conscious admissions
facts.source: Supreme Court of the United States, 600 U.S. 181 (2023)

items.stem: In high school sports, which rule comes closest to your view for transgender girls?
items.scope: Think about competitive school teams, not casual or intramural play.
options: They should be able to play on girls' teams
They should be able to play on girls' teams if they meet medical criteria, such as hormone levels
They should play on boys' teams or in an open category, not girls' teams

definitions.text: Students who were identified as male at birth and identify as girls.

items.stem: If a federal court rules that something a president did is illegal, what should the president do?
items.scope: Answer for any president of either party, now or in the future.
options: Comply fully while appealing, and avoid attacking the judge
Comply while appealing, but criticize the judge publicly
Comply only if a higher court agrees with the ruling
Ignore the ruling if the president believes it is wrong

items.stem: When Congress passes a major law, how often do you think its main purpose is to help the public rather than donors or party leaders?
items.scope: Think about Congress in general, under either party's control.
options: Almost always (9 or more times in 10)
Most of the time (about 7 in 10)
About half the time
Sometimes (about 3 in 10)
Rarely (1 in 10 or less)

items.stem: If another country attacks a US ally, what should the US usually do?
items.scope: Think about an ally the US has a formal defense agreement with, such as a NATO member.
options: Send US troops to help defend it
Send weapons and money, but not troops
Impose sanctions on the attacker and send humanitarian aid, but not weapons
Stay out of it

definitions.text: A treaty in which the US has promised to help defend another country, such as the North Atlantic Treaty (NATO).

items.stem: "When government tries to solve a social problem, it usually makes things worse."
items.scope: Use the meanings shown for each answer.
options: Strongly disagree
Disagree
Torn
Agree
Strongly agree
point_meanings: False in nearly every case I can think of
False in most cases, with some real exceptions
I can see it both ways about equally
True in most cases, with some real exceptions
True in nearly every case I can think of

items.stem: "Some social problems are too big to be solved without the federal government."
items.scope: Use the meanings shown for each answer.
options: Strongly agree
Agree
Torn
Disagree
Strongly disagree
point_meanings: True in nearly every case I can think of
True in most cases, with some real exceptions
I can see it both ways about equally
False in most cases, with some real exceptions
False in nearly every case I can think of
